title: Ventilator alarm
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Respond to a ventilator alarm by going to the patient first.
Secure ventilation before troubleshooting the machine.
Recognise that alarm limits and modes are changed only with authority.

sources.use: manufacturer manual: alarm and alternative ventilation statements for that device only

required_sources: Cross-manufacturer alarm-management guidance and the unit's alarm policy
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
Device-specific alarm behaviour differs by manufacturer and software; the scenario uses generic wording.
Alarm causes and lists are deliberately not reproduced.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
setting: A fictional ventilated adult on a fictional unit; the ventilator is a generic device.

steps.info: A high-pressure alarm sounds on a ventilated patient's machine. The patient is coughing and looks uncomfortable.

options.text: Go to the patient and look at the patient, the airway, the circuit and the machine.
options.feedback: Going to the patient is the expected response to every alarm, and the machine's message guides but does not replace looking at the patient.
options.consequence: You find the patient coughing against the ventilator and a kink in the circuit near the tube.

options.text: Silence the alarm and finish the task you were doing.
options.feedback: Silencing is not a response; the problem persists and the alarm will return.
options.consequence: The alarm sounds again and the patient's saturation has fallen.

options.text: Widen the alarm limits so the alarm stops.
options.feedback: Alarm limits and modes are changed only when authorised by order, protocol and training; extreme limits make alarms useless.
options.consequence: The alarm stops but the cause remains, and the patient's saturation falls unnoticed.

steps.info: The patient's saturation is falling and the chest is not moving well. You cannot find a quick cause.
steps.prompt: What is the right next step?

options.text: Use the unit's emergency ventilation method (for example a manual resuscitation bag) and call for help.
options.feedback: If ventilation is inadequate and the cause is not immediately correctable, provide alternative ventilation and call for help; the equipment to use is local policy.
options.consequence: The patient is ventilated by hand and the team arrives to find and correct the problem.

options.text: Keep troubleshooting the machine on your own.
options.feedback: Staying with the machine while the patient is inadequately ventilated delays rescue.
options.consequence: The patient's condition worsens before help arrives.

options.text: Change the ventilator mode yourself to see if the patient improves.
options.feedback: Modes and settings are changed only with authority and competence.
options.consequence: The new mode does not help and the team must now also work out what was changed.

steps.info: The team has corrected the problem and the patient is stable on the ventilator again.

options.text: Give a clear SBAR handover of what happened and document the event and your actions.
options.feedback: A structured handover and a record of events and responses keep the team informed and support learning.
options.consequence: The next shift knows what happened and checks the circuit position at each round.

options.text: Document only that the alarm sounded.
options.feedback: An incomplete record loses the cause, the actions and the outcome.
options.consequence: The next shift sees an alarm but no explanation and repeats the troubleshooting.

options.text: Reset the alarm limits to the narrowest settings so any change will alarm.
options.feedback: Limits are set by order or protocol, not by the nurse's own choice.
options.consequence: The limits cause frequent false alarms and the team asks who changed them.

learning_points: Every alarm is answered at the patient first.
If ventilation is inadequate and not quickly fixable, give alternative ventilation and call for help.
Do not silence alarms as a response or change limits and modes without authority.
Record and hand over what happened.
